text: The MID Server you just met solves one problem: reaching systems a cloud instance can't see. This lesson covers the three real jobs that actually get routed through it — Discovery, Orchestration, and relaying integrations to internal-only systems.

Discovery is the most common use case: scanning a customer's internal network to find and catalog configuration items — servers, network devices, applications — and populating the CMDB. A dedicated course later in this catalog covers Discovery in full depth; here, what matters is that the MID Server is the only thing actually inside the network able to probe those addresses. Orchestration works the same way, running automation against on-prem systems the cloud instance has no path to reach directly.

The use case most relevant to everything built in this course is the relay pattern. An IntegrationHub action or REST Message that needs to reach an internal-only system is still configured exactly as Chapters 2 through 5 taught — same REST Message record, same authentication profile, same connector action.

The one thing that changes is a single setting: the connection and credential alias gets pointed at a specific MID Server. When the integration runs, the actual outbound HTTP call fires from inside the customer's network, launched by the MID Server, instead of from ServiceNow's cloud. The instance never needs a direct network path to the target at all.

Not every integration in Chapter 8's capstone will need a MID Server — plenty of real targets have public endpoints. But recognizing when one sits behind a firewall, and knowing the fix is a routing selection rather than a redesign, is exactly the judgment the capstone expects. Next: Capstone Kickoff, defining the integration requirements.
